Society & Human Rights
• Authorities in Austria, Germany and Hungary are probing reports of sharp objects inserted into Halloween sweets, including a child injured by a pin hidden in chocolate.
• In South Africa’s local elections, frustration over poor public services is fueling pressure on the ANC amid signs of voter discontent.
• Abdul El-Sayed’s win in Michigan makes him the first Muslim senator in U.S. history, a landmark for representation.
• UK policies face challenges: activists appeal the proscription of Palestine Action, and UNHCR warns the UK’s proposed 30-year “earned settlement” for refugees raises serious concerns.
• Protests across Europe and in London highlight ongoing tensions over civil rights, austerity and cultural controversies, including demonstrations at a new “Harry Potter” store.
Why it matters: Public safety scares, service delivery failures, and contested policies are intensifying social strains while electoral milestones reshape representation.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Democrats seized full control of Congress in the U.S. midterms, triggering international reactions and recalculations on Iran, Ukraine and wider foreign policy.
• Iran’s leaders hailed U.S. voters “rejecting war,” while warning hostility persists; European officials framed the result as a rebuke of Trumpism.
• Kyiv-linked assets rose on expectations of closer U.S.-Ukraine ties; the EU plans talks with Washington and partners on sustaining support for Ukraine.
• Rwanda’s army team was removed from the Africa basketball league due to U.S. sanctions over its role in DR Congo.
• Analysts say Democrats can block parts of Trump’s agenda but face veto constraints, setting up two years of constitutional brinkmanship.
Why it matters: A shift in U.S. legislative power reverberates across global alliances and conflicts, reshaping policy trajectories and market expectations.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmr4y92rgd9po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
https://www.ft.com/content/97070d8f-ce2d-4873-8c70-cc8338f7ce1c?syn-25a6b1a6=1

Armed Conflict & Security
• A U.S. contractor admitted sharing classified information to aid Ethiopian operations against Tigray fighters, underscoring insider threats and conflict spillovers.
• Israeli strikes hit Gaza displacement camps as mass arrests swept the occupied West Bank, with 45 detained, Al Jazeera reports.
• The Indian Navy rescued 20 crew from an Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia amid reports of resurging piracy.
• France’s national blood service says hackers altered temperature thresholds at three blood cold stores in an escalation of attacks on critical infrastructure.
• Ukraine’s drone campaign is prompting Russia to explore underground data centers; meanwhile, firms propose defensive cubesats for space-based assets.
Why it matters: Hybrid warfare, cyberattacks on health systems, and maritime piracy highlight widening security risks that challenge civilian resilience and infrastructure.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y8lz73vmv7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

Sports
• Rafael Nadal is set to join Real Madrid’s board, extending his influence from tennis into football governance.
• Tributes continue for Tenerife’s Jesús de Miguel after his fatal on-pitch collision; Andorra’s goalkeeper says he is “deeply affected” and would never intentionally harm anyone.
• West Ham appointed Scott Parker as head coach on a two-and-a-half-year deal.
• Rory McIlroy says LIV Golf aimed to “destroy the European Tour” months before filing for bankruptcy protection.
Why it matters: Leadership shifts, tragedy responses, and unresolved tensions in golf reflect the evolving dynamics and ethics of elite sport.

Other
• Investigators found tail components miles from a Florida Learjet crash site, confirming the plane was breaking apart before impact.
• Fashion label Coperni closed following a breakdown with its distributor, highlighting risks in brand-partner relationships.
Why it matters: Aviation safety findings and fashion industry ruptures point to the importance of robust oversight and partnerships.

https://www.vogue.com/article/coperni-closes-following-relationship-breakdown-with-distributor

Science & Technology
• A UEFI bootkit dubbed BlackX infected fully patched Windows machines, reigniting debate over Secure Boot clarity and firmware-layer defenses.
• NASA is seeking industry ideas to extend Hubble’s lifespan as the telescope experiences orbital drag; stargazers can catch peak Taurids with potential fireballs.
• SpaceX struck a multi-year deal with Qualcomm to build base stations for its Starlink Mobile network, expanding space-to-ground connectivity.
• Finland’s Onkalo nuclear waste repository, designed to last 100,000 years, is set to begin operations—an engineering milestone for long-term safety.
Why it matters: Critical infrastructure security, enduring space science, and long-horizon engineering decisions shape trust and capabilities in tech.
https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/uefi-bootkit-infected-fully-patched-windows-machines-is-microsoft-to-blame/
https://www.space.com/astronomy/hubble-space-telescope/nasa-asks-industry-for-ideas-about-saving-hubble-space-telescope

Artificial Intelligence
• Google will fully disable Search for K-12 accounts in schools that opt out of AI, escalating debates on AI in education and access to core tools.
• Apple opened Siri AI to third-party apps and introduced ambient “Audio Intelligence” on Apple Watch, while Netflix launched an “AI Discover” tab for mood-based recommendations.
• OpenAI says ChatGPT search queries are now a substantial share of Google’s volume; Nexus Mods will require AI disclosures on uploads.
• The New York Times sued Brave over paywall tools and alleged AI content deals; Anthropic unveiled “FlashProve” to verify model identities; CrowdStrike touted a kill switch for rogue AI agents.
• Researchers showed language models can screen for Parkinson’s across diverse questionnaires, hinting at scalable, low-cost health assessments.
Why it matters: Platform changes, governance and legal battles, and emerging safety tools are defining how AI is integrated, regulated, and trusted.
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1025411/google-turn-off-search-ai-features
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1025694/apple-siri-ai-third-party-apps

Economy & Markets
• U.S. stocks and European bank shares rebounded after Democrats’ sweep, though strategists caution gains are typically muted after similar midterm outcomes.
• Tech earnings were mixed: AMD surged on AI chip demand, Apple fell on memory cost pressures; Palantir’s stock slid on contract value concerns.
• The UK revised down a claim that AI would add £400 billion to the economy, with officials noting slower adoption than expected.
• Regulators will scrutinize Sky’s $2.1B ITV deal after a public interest notice; Africa launched a long-delayed energy bank focused on fossil projects.
• Airlines and mobility firms flagged cost pressures: SunExpress trimmed winter capacity amid higher jet fuel prices; Uber beat revenue estimates despite unit headwinds.
Why it matters: Political shifts, AI economics, and sector-specific cost dynamics are driving market rotations and regulatory focus.

Entertainment
• Tokyo International Film Festival awarded its top prize to “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” while a Tarantino interview revived interest in a non-made Cliff Booth sequel.
• Gaming headlines: GTA VI will require up to 212GB of storage; indie devs say Steam review backlogs are delaying launches; Nintendo set for an Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2.
• Music and live events: Ozzfest 2027 teased a major announcement; Katseye postponed a Detroit show due to illness; Starbucks dropped its first holiday album in over a decade.
• Fashion and culture: Palace unveiled a London flagship-only Burberry capsule; Vogue tracked industry funding amid fresh product drops.
• Viral misinformation: “hair transplant” photos of Jeff Bezos and Jason Statham were debunked as AI fakes.
Why it matters: Festivals, platform logistics, and brand collaborations intersect with misinformation risks, shaping how audiences discover and trust culture.

Art & Culture
• Car interiors are trending back toward tactile buttons and ample storage, designers say, as usability concerns trump glossy minimalism.
• Australia launched a National Songbook to preserve culturally defining tracks, from “Beds Are Burning” to “Friday on My Mind.”
• Palace’s new London flagship leans into stained glass and archive displays, blurring retail and museum aesthetics; a BAFTA Breakthrough honoree highlighted sign language’s impact on film craft.
Why it matters: Design preferences, heritage preservation, and experiential retail reflect evolving cultural values and access.
https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/11/yes-to-storage-no-to-piano-black-how-car-interior-design-is-changing/
https://www.billboard.com/music/awards/first-songs-inducted-into-australia-national-songbook-1236373819/

Health & Pandemic
• A child’s measles death reignited concerns about vaccine hesitancy as NY officials criticized anti-vaccine activism; reports say a CDC alert was delayed.
• Great Britain’s worst bluetongue season is straining farmers and animal welfare, MPs were told.
• AI models (Quest2Dx) showed promise in screening Parkinson’s disease using questionnaire data; Hailey Bieber discussed postnatal PMDD challenges.
• Commentary warned mink farms could incubate pandemic-level flu strains without stronger safeguards.
Why it matters: Vaccine uptake, zoonotic and animal health risks, and AI-enabled screening are key fronts in public health resilience.
https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/another-child-dies-of-measles-as-cdc-reportedly-holds-up-health-alert/
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/03/great-britain-worst-ever-bluetongue-season-major-animal-welfare-crisis

Climate & Environment
• New Delhi’s air pollution surged to over 30x WHO limits, underscoring persistent urban air quality crises.
• Brazil’s COP30 roadmaps aim to halt deforestation by 2030 and sketch a first global fossil timetable; Carbon Brief recapped COP17 biodiversity outcomes; the UK’s climate minister urged COP31 to face “really scary” science.
• Ireland’s sea levels show marked acceleration over the past century; Kashmir’s traditional potato pits are vanishing, risking local varieties and knowledge.
• Data centers are turning to old jet engines to meet power needs as grid waits lengthen; researchers say penguin guano fuels algae that increases snow melt.
Why it matters: Policy pathways, extreme pollution, and unconventional energy stopgaps reveal the urgency—and complexity—of climate adaptation and mitigation.
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-toxic-air-pollution-surges-indian.html
https://www.climatechangenews.com/2026/11/03/brazils-fossil-fuel-roadmap-sketches-out-first-global-timetable/

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• The gut microbiome’s age-driven shifts may drive inflammation and organ dysfunction, making it a central lever for healthy aging.
• Researchers propose “ferro-aging” as distinct from ferroptosis, calling for targeted interventions to validate its role in age-related disease.
• Activating mitofusins extended lifespan in nematode worms, supporting mitochondrial dynamics as a therapeutic target.
• Male mice showed earlier loss of anti-cancer immunity tied to declining naïve T cells; a Nature Aging piece called for clearer framing of menopause transitions.
Why it matters: Pinpointing mechanisms—from microbes to mitochondria and immune aging—could enable therapies that meaningfully extend healthy lifespan.

Science & Technology.title: IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts
Science & Technology.text: To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.Technical discussions grounded in engineeringRather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.Extending access through a virtual formatThe organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.Examining governed AI agentsThe most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.Building a continuing technical programFuture sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Entertainment.title: 8 Drops You Don’t Want to Miss This Week
Entertainment.text: With another week upon us, we have yet another installment of our product drops series.This week’s lineup kicks off with Supreme teaming up with Vaquera on a campy Fall 2026 capsule that stretches from graphic hoodies to a duvet set. Fear of God follows by tapping Jon Bernthal to front the campaign for The Eternal Order, while BAPE and adidas enlist Jalen Williams for a Y2K hoops collection led by the Crazy Energy+. In London, Palace Skateboards celebrates its new Poland Street flagship with a store-exclusive Burberry capsule, and back in Los Angeles, Crenshaw Skate Club and Sprite turn South Central barbershop culture into a nostalgic streetwear range. Pas Normal Studios and Salomon reunite for a sixth running capsule built for cyclists in the off-season, and Kith brings TUMI back through its Monday Program for a third run of ombré aluminum luggage. Last but not least, The North Face and Cecilie Bahnsen deliver a romantic fourth chapter headlined by a cropped, floral-embroidered Nuptse.Check out this week’s 8 drops you don’t want to miss below.Supreme x Vaquera Fall 2026 Collaboration CollectionSupreme has partnered with Vaquera, the New York-founded, Paris-based label led by Patric DiCaprio and Bryn Taubensee, on a Fall 2026 capsule that brings the label’s irreverent, outsider-minded take on American staples into Supreme’s world. The range centers on the Christ and Kisses zip-up hoodies, a Collage long sleeve top with matching loose-fit jeans, basketball shorts and the Bra and Mannequin tees, alongside a co-branded Box Logo New Era fitted. A Supreme/Vaquera Collage duvet and pillow set carries the collaboration into the bedroom. The collection releases November 5 via Supreme’s flagship stores and online, with an Asia launch following on November 7.Fear of God “The Eternal Order” CollectionFear of God has enlisted Jon Bernthal to front the campaign for The Eternal Order, the tenth full expression of Jerry Lorenzo’s codified system of dressing. Framed as a lasting standard rather than a seasonal offering, the range leans on disciplined tailoring, restrained proportions and a dialogue between archival silhouettes and contemporary construction. The campaign places Bernthal against a sweeping, elemental landscape, with Lorenzo pointing to the actor’s grounded sense of purpose as a reflection of the house’s own values. The Eternal Order is available now via Fear of God online and select global retailers.adidas x BAPE Collabadidas and BAPE have reunited for a basketball collection rooted in the late-’90s and early-2000s era, fronted by NBA standout Jalen Williams. The footwear centerpiece is the Crazy Energy+, one of adidas Basketball’s newest performance models, finished in an all-over metallic “COLOR CAMO SILVER” print with a knitted “WGM” lace overlay and two sets of interchangeable laces. The apparel leans on BAPE’s “COLOR CAMO PURPLE” across a reversible mesh shark hoodie and reversible Adibreak track pants, while a black varsity jacket with purple paneling, gold studs and a chenille “World Gone Mad” back graphic serves as the statement piece. A warm-up top, BABY MILO tee, reversible knit beanie and BABY MILO basketball bag round out the range. The collection launches November 7 via the adidas CONFIRMED app, select retailers, BAPE STORE locations and BAPE.COM.Palace Skateboards x Burberry CapsulePalace Skateboards is marking the opening of its new Poland Street flagship in London with a 10-piece Burberry capsule. The Palace Burberry Camden car coat leads the way in honey beige with screen-printed artwork inspired by the British countryside, joined by a cashmere scarf that weaves both brands’ logos into the signature Burberry Check. The House Check also runs across a cap, a shirt, short- and long-sleeve tees, a hooded jacket and a skate deck, while a polo with an embroidered Poland Street graphic nods directly to the new store. Palace is also releasing its own London-exclusive range, led by a Gore-Tex jacket and embossed throughout with the number 8 from the flagship’s address. Both releases are available exclusively in-store at the Poland Street flagship, which opens November 5.Crenshaw Skate Club x Sprite CollectionCrenshaw Skate Club and Sprite have teamed up on a capsule that merges the label’s skate roots with the soda brand’s longstanding ties to basketball and street culture. Rendered in Sprite’s green and yellow, the lineup spans graphic tees, sweatpants, a six-panel cap and an updated tracksuit that pairs a mesh track jacket with baggy mesh shorts. Founder Tobey McIntosh drew on his South Central upbringing for standout pieces such as a tee showing a portrait with the Sprite logo shaved into the hair, inspired by the haircut charts he remembers from neighborhood barbershops. The collection debuts November 7 at a pop-up at 439 N Fairfax Avenue in Los Angeles, the former Supreme store that first stocked the brand in 2018, before releasing globally on November 9 at 11 a.m. PST via the brand’s website, with prices ranging from $50 to $120 USD.Pas Normal Studios x Salomon CollectionPas Normal Studios and Salomon have reunited for their sixth collaboration, a three-piece cold-weather capsule designed for cyclists moving into distance running during the off-season. Leading the release is the AERO BLAZE 4 GRVL GORE-TEX, a mixed-terrain daily trainer that pairs Salomon’s lightweight cushioning and multi-surface grip with a fully waterproof GORE-TEX membrane, finished in PNS’s understated color direction. The GRAVEL CONCEPT 2 hydration vest and lightweight S/LAB BELT complete the lineup, offering stable, bounce-free storage for longer routes. The collection releases November 5 via Pas Normal Studios, Salomon, Pas Normal Studios flagship stores and select global retailers.Kith for TUMI 2026 CollectionKith and TUMI have reconnected for a third collaboration, released through Kith’s weekly Monday Program. The capsule reworks TUMI’s 19 Degree Aluminum Carry-On in three ombré finishes: Astro, which fades from charcoal to taupe; Majestic, in deep slate teal; and Rogue, in dusty rose. Each one carries a tonal Kith pattern across its ridged shell, plus a matching lining, a co-branded leather patch and packing cubes. Every colorway is paired with its own aluminum accessory, namely a cedar-lined Travel Cigar Case for Astro, a magnetic Sunglass Case for Majestic and a three-slot Watch Case for Rogue. The collection released November 2 at 11 a.m. EST via Kith’s Monday Program, as well as at Kith Tokyo, Kith Osaka, JP.Kith.com and the Kith App, with prices starting at $395 USD for the Sunglass Case, $595 USD each for the Cigar and Watch Cases and $1,495 USD per Carry-On.The North Face x Cecilie Bahnsen FW26 CollectionThe North Face and Copenhagen designer Cecilie Bahnsen have reunited for a fourth chapter, a seven-piece collection first previewed on Bahnsen’s Fall/Winter 2026 runway at Paris Fashion Week. Offered in TNF Black and Midnight Sky, the range softens technical mountain staples with lace stitching and dimensional floral embroidery. It’s led by the Lucia Nuptse Short Jacket, a cropped take on the iconic puffer covered in three-dimensional Superpose blossoms. The lineup also includes the Sofia Insulated Crew Neck Top, Symone Dotknit Top, Meghan Small Crevasse Cinch Bag and Amalia Waist Pack, along with the Martina Verto Alpine Mid boot and Angela ThermoBall Mule. The collection dropped November 2 on Cecilie Bahnsen’s website, with a wider release via The North Face and select retailers on November 5.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Asake Came Out In Two Bespoke Levi’s Looks At Headline London Show
Entertainment.text: Asake returned to The O2 Arena after his debut show there three years ago, marking his third sold-out headline at the 20,000-capacity venue in London.Supporting his fourth studio album, M$NEY, which dropped earlier this year as his first project released through his independent imprint Giran Republic, the Nigerian artist has been embarking on his In God We Trust World Tour.Lauded as the sonic evolution of his catalog, the project showcases his creative maturity, merging Afropop, amapiano and jazz, while lyrics draw on cultural folklore, spirituality and religious symbolism. With features from French artists Tiakola and DJ Snake, as well as South African DJ Kabza de Small, it proves how global the Afrobeats sound has travelled. And upon its launch, M$NEY broke the record for the most first-week streams in Spotify Nigeria history. Speaking to Hypebeast, he explains, “The music carries the experiences, the mindset, and the energy of a particular time in my life. With the In God We Trust World Tour, I want people to experience that energy in a way that goes beyond listening to the songs.”"When I’m on stage, I’m thinking about how the music makes people feel, how we connect, and how we bring that feeling into the room."Stepping on stage at his sold-out show, Asake sported two custom Levi’s® outfits, with concepts created by Kevin Mukuri and Mariam Afolabi, looks by Niran Nair, all completely embellished with rhinestones by London-based artisans AGR Knit, and over 200 hours of craftsmanship going into the combined looks.The first outfit was produced with premium Japanese white denim curated by the brand’s Lot 1 in-house ateliers, with each garment individually cut from bespoke patterns for the two-piece. The look incorporates 100,000 all-over hand-applied crystals, with “GIRAN” lettering on the back, as well as signature Levi’s® detailing, including The Red Tab, arcuate stitching and Two-Horse back patch.The second look takes the Levi’s® Engineered Moto Jacket from the early 2000s as its foundation. Adorned in 40,000 crystals and constructed using premium blue Kaihara denim, and treated eco-consciously by London-based specialists Laundre using laser technology to create an ombre effect, it features custom “GIRAN” lettering emblazoned on the back, laurel shoulder details, and leather piping. While underneath, a rhinestone-clad Levi’s® Batwing tee features the red-tab logo on the chest and “M$NEY” on the opposite side.Hypebeast caught up with Asake ahead of the show to discuss fashion inspirations, sound evolution and In God We Trust.Hypebeast: How would you describe your personal style, and how has it evolved alongside your music?Asake: My style has always been connected to who I am and where I come from. As the music has grown, I’ve become more open to exploring different things and expressing myself in new ways. But growth doesn’t mean you have to become somebody else. I still want to see myself in what I wear. For me, it’s about evolving while staying true to the person I’ve always been.When putting a look together, what inspires you? Is it a feeling, a reference, or a story you want to tell?It starts with a feeling. I like to trust my own instincts and create from a place that feels natural to me. I’m not trying to recreate what somebody else has done. I want to explore what I see in my mind and bring that to life. Sometimes I know exactly what I want, and sometimes I discover it along the way. I think originality comes from being comfortable enough with yourself to follow your own vision.How does the music from M$NEY shape the energy and creative direction of the In God We Trust World Tour, and how do you bring that sound to life on stage?The music carries the experiences, the mindset, and the energy of a particular time in my life. With the In God We Trust World Tour, I want people to experience that energy in a way that goes beyond listening to the songs. When I’m on stage, I’m thinking about how the music makes people feel, how we connect, and how we bring that feeling into the room. Every performance is different because the people, the place, and the moment are different. That’s what makes performing special to me.Walk us through the look you’re wearing. What drew you to these pieces, and why does this look feel like you?I’m drawn to pieces that have their own character. I like when something has a strong identity but still gives me room to make it my own. With this look, it’s about the way the pieces come together and how I feel wearing them. I don’t want to feel like I’m playing a character. Even when I’m experimenting with something different, it has to feel natural to me. That’s when I know a look is right.What was important to you in creating this exclusive collaboration with Levi’s, and how did you make it your own?It was important that the collaboration felt genuine. Levi’s has a history and an identity of its own, and I wanted to bring my perspective into that without losing what makes the brand special. I’m always interested in taking something and expressing it in a way that feels personal. I wanted the collaboration to reflect how I see things, not just put my name on something. When I create, I want people to feel that there was a real intention behind it.How do you approach dressing for the stage versus your everyday life?On stage, I think about the full experience. The clothes have to connect with the music, the movement, and the energy I want to give the audience. Outside of that, I dress more according to how I feel. I don’t always want to think too much about it. But in both spaces, I want to feel comfortable in myself. The stage allows me to explore a different side of my expression, but it doesn’t mean I have to become somebody different.Denim has a long history in music and streetwear. What does it mean to you, and how do you make it feel personal?What I like about denim is that it doesn’t belong to just one person or one generation. It has been part of so many different cultures and expressions, but everybody can bring something different to it. For me, making it personal is about how you wear it and what you bring to it. You don’t always need to change something completely to make it your own. Sometimes, the difference is in the way you see it.What do you hope your style communicates about who you are as an artist today?I hope it shows that I’m not afraid to be myself or to keep evolving. I’ve learned that you don’t have to explain everything about who you are through what you wear or the music you make. Sometimes, people will understand you through the feeling you give them. I want my style to reflect where I am in my life while leaving room for where I’m going. I know who I am, but I’m still discovering different sides of myself, and I think that’s part of being an artist.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Adding a fourth monkey, 'do no evil', to the classic symbol, the brands have built a unique concept that translates this philosophical and visual essence into modern technical gear.The lineup includes a wide range of items, from a set-up featuring fur details to a packable jacket, hoodie, T-shirts, hats, and gloves. Additionally, some items incorporate four beads symbolizing the four monkeys as a shared detail, bringing a sense of unity to the entire collection.The released campaign visuals depict humans and monkey-like beings coexisting in everyday scenes without acknowledging each other. Entertainment.title: PLEASURES’ Holiday 2026 “Ciel Couvert” Collection Is Built for Overcast Days
Entertainment.text: SummaryPLEASURES has unveiled its Holiday 2026 collection, “Ciel Couvert,” which takes its name from the French phrase for an overcast skyDark neutrals tie together a lineup of graphic pieces, knitwear, outerwear, denim, headwear and bottomsThe campaign was photographed in Montreal by Aime-Elle, with art direction from Nikki NixonPLEASURES has unveiled its Holiday 2026 collection, “Ciel Couvert,” taking its name from the French phrase for an overcast sky. The Los Angeles label leans fully into that gray-weather mood, building the season around a deeper, moodier palette and a heavy rotation of layering pieces made for colder months.Dark neutrals act as the anchor for the entire range, giving even the louder graphic pieces a shared tonal base. Against that backdrop, PLEASURES works through a spread of knitwear in different constructions, alongside cold-weather layers designed to stack rather than stand alone.The category mix runs wide, covering outerwear, denim, headwear and a broad selection of bottoms. Rather than relying on new shapes, the collection takes recognizable silhouettes and gives them a different edge through careful detailing, pairing heavier and lighter fabrics, smooth and rough surfaces, and print-led pieces with pared-back everyday staples. Proportions shift from piece to piece as well, setting up contrast within a single outfit.Montreal serves as the collection’s visual counterpart. The campaign, shot across the city by photographer Aime-Elle, plays on the contrast between Montreal’s architectural styles, its varied textures and its own subdued color story, framing the clothes as part of the streetscape rather than placed in front of it. Nikki Nixon handled art direction, while Sara Takenaka styled and produced the shoot, with Aljosa Alijagic assisting on photography.The result is a collection where the setting and the garments share the same language. The rough surfaces and tonal shifts of the city echo the textural layering of the clothes, extending the overcast idea from the palette into the campaign imagery itself.The PLEASURES Holiday 2026 “Ciel Couvert” collection is available now via PLEASURES and select global retailers.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Palace Skateboards Brings Burberry Home for Its London Flagship-Only Capsule
Entertainment.text: SummaryPalace Skateboards and Burberry have created a 10-piece capsule to celebrate the opening of Palace’s new London flagshipThe collaboration pairs a screen-printed honey beige car coat with a run of pieces in Burberry’s House CheckPalace is also releasing its own limited London-exclusive range, with every item embossed with the number 8Palace Skateboards and Burberry have teamed up on a 10-piece capsule to celebrate the opening of Palace’s new London flagship, arriving alongside a limited London-exclusive range from Palace itself. Together, the two releases turn the November 5 opening into a hometown event, uniting the city’s skate institution with one of Britain’s most recognizable heritage houses.The Palace Burberry Camden car coat leads the collaboration, cut in honey beige and finished with screen-printed artwork inspired by the British countryside. It’s joined by a cashmere scarf in the signature Burberry Check, woven with both the Palace logo and the Burberry label, giving the two brands equal billing on a single accessory.Burberry’s House Check carries the remainder of the capsule, appearing on a baseball cap, a shirt, short- and long-sleeve T-shirts, a hooded jacket and a board. A polo shirt rounds things out with an embroidered Poland Street graphic, the one piece in the lineup that speaks directly to the new store.Palace’s own London-exclusive range takes a more personal route, built around the number 8 from the flagship’s Poland Street address. A Gore-Tex jacket anchors the lineup, backed by hoodies, T-shirts, a cap, a tote and further accessories, each embossed with the numeral. An infinity symbol runs throughout the collection as a subtle callback to the Palace logo, keeping the range in step with the brand’s established visual language.Burberry is the latest British name to join a collaborator list that already includes Vivienne Westwood, Fred Perry and Barbour, alongside global partners such as Nike and Gucci. Founded in 2009 by Lev Tanju and Gareth Skewis, Palace has grown from an underground skate label into a global streetwear force, and opening a London flagship with a Burberry tie-up puts that British lineage front and center.The Palace Skateboards x Burberry capsule is available exclusively at Palace’s Poland Street flagship, which opens November 5.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Palace Skateboard's Newest London Flagship Is a Stained-Glass Museum Built From Its Own Archive
Art & Culture.text: SummaryPalace Skateboards is opening a 250.6-square-metre London flagship on Poland Street that borrows from the British Museum and the stained glass of British churchesArchive photographs and references to the brand’s original shop are displayed like museum exhibits, framed by oversized stained-glass windows carrying Palace artworkFurniture and fixtures nod to Manor Place and Brewer Street, while an LED video wall rises through both floors of the storePalace Skateboards is opening its new Poland Street flagship in London on Thursday, November 5, setting its skate-bred identity inside a space modeled on two pillars of British architecture. The design pulls from the grand, institutional feel of the British Museum and the stained-glass windows of the country’s churches, then filters both through Palace’s own graphic vocabulary so the store reads as equal parts city landmark and brand time capsule.The storefront’s oversized windows do the heaviest lifting, recast as stained-glass panels carrying Palace artwork and treated as a gallery installation in their own right. Inside, the museum framing carries through, with photographs pulled from the Palace archive and references to the brand’s first shop presented as curated exhibits rather than background decor.Raw and refined materials play off each other throughout the 250.6-square-metre interior. Concrete and galvanized steel lay down an industrial base, softened by light oak panelling, parquet floors and crisp white walls, while P-shaped marble tiles replicate the ones used in the original Palace shop. Unfinished stone plinths act as display points around the floor, a mirrored deck wall greets shoppers at the door, and recessed deck displays are set directly into the concrete columns as standalone art pieces.Much of the furniture doubles as a history lesson for anyone who has followed the brand from the start. A raw oak bench and stool take the shape of the Tri-ferg, Victoria benches point back to Manor Place, and a Rolls-Royce grille carried over from the original store pays tribute to Brewer Street. Even the entrance gets a custom touch in the form of a door handle rendered in Palace artwork, while a large LED video wall climbs from the ground floor to the first, stitching the two levels together visually.Poland Street is the newest stop in a retail footprint that already spans New York, Los Angeles, Tokyo, Osaka, Fukuoka, Apgujeong, Hongdae, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Singapore. Founded in 2009 by Lev Tanju and Gareth Skewis, Palace has grown from an underground skate label into a global name, and its approach to retail has followed suit, building each store as a destination shaped by its city while leaning on the brand’s own archive.The Palace Skateboards Poland Street flagship opens Thursday, November 5.Palace Skateboards Poland Street Flagship8 Poland StLondon, W1F 8PXClick here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Could it be the spot where the next pandemic begins? It’s certainly a candidate, not least because the chain of events that could trigger a plague far worse than Covid-19 looks like the opening sequence of a disaster movie. A really bad disaster movie, in which the levels of carelessness and turpitude defy belief.A report by the investigative news service ProPublica reveals that bird flu has been raging in a mink farm in Utah since August, and it appears next to nothing has been done by public officials. In 2023, I warned in the Guardian that mink farms could scarcely be better designed to generate lethal plagues. This is for three reasons: mink are fed on the offcuts of chickens, cows and other farm animals, in which new viral variants often develop; mink readily host both avian and human flu viruses, which can then exchange genetic material, turning a bird disease into a human one; and mink possess extremely high “zoonotic potential” – the ability to infect animals of other species, including human beings.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
